rows.speaker: الجبائي
rows.claim: Al-Jubbāʾī argues that the Prophet’s disavowal of their sins entails God’s disavowal too; otherwise God would contradict His Messenger, and a God who disavows their acts cannot create or will them.
rows.anchor: قال الجبائي هذا يدل على أنه عليه السلام كان بريئا من معاصيهم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Rāzī answers that God disavows sins by forbidding rather than commanding them, but does will their occurrence: His knowledge of an event makes it necessary, and the necessary cannot be willed not to occur.
rows.anchor: أنه تعالى بريء من المعاصي بمعنى أنه ما أمر بها بل نهى عنها

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Tawakkul is entrusting one’s affair to someone who controls it and can bring benefit or harm.
rows.anchor: والتوكل عبارة عن تفويض الرجل أمره إلى من يملك أمره ويقدر على نفعه وضره

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The Mighty crushes the Prophet’s enemies by His might, and the Merciful helps him against them through His mercy.
rows.anchor: على الذي يقهر أعداءك بعزته وينصرك عليهم برحمته

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: One interpretation is the Prophet’s night worship and his movement among the worshippers; “those prostrating” means the worshippers.
rows.anchor: المراد ما كان يفعله في جوف الليل من قيامه للتهجد

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: An anonymous report says that after the night vigil ceased to be obligatory, the Prophet visited his Companions’ homes that night to see their worship, hearing them hum with remembrance like wasps in their nests; Rāzī gives no grading.
rows.anchor: كما يحكى أنه حين نسخ فرض قيام الليل طاف تلك الليلة ببيوت أصحابه لينظر ما يصنعون

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A second interpretation is that the Prophet rises to lead the congregation and moves among the worshippers in standing, bowing, prostration, and sitting.
rows.anchor: المعنى يراك حين تقوم للصلاة بالناس جماعة وتقلبه في الساجدين تصرفه فيما بينهم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A third interpretation is that God never misses the Prophet’s state whenever he rises or moves among the worshippers while managing religious affairs.
rows.anchor: أنه لا يخفى عليه حالك كلما قمت وتقلبت مع الساجدين في كفاية أمور الدين

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A fourth interpretation takes the Prophet’s “movement” as his gaze moving among those behind him, since he said that he saw them from behind while they prayed.
rows.anchor: المراد تقلب بصره فيمن ( يلي ) خلفه

rows.speaker: النبي صلى الله عليه وسلم
rows.claim: Rāzī cites Muhammad’s statement, “Complete bowing and prostration; by God, I see you from behind”; he gives no grading.
rows.anchor: من قوله صلى الله عليه وسلم : ( أتموا الركوع والسجود فوالله إني لأراكم من خلفي )

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: “The All-Hearing” concerns what the Prophet says; “the All-Knowing” concerns what he intends and does.
rows.anchor: العليم } أي بما تنويه وتعمله

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Hearing is a distinct divine attribute from knowledge of things heard; otherwise “All-Knowing” would add nothing to “All-Hearing.”
rows.anchor: كونه سميعا أمر مغاير لعلمه بالمسموعات

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Rāzī notes a reading with the first-person plural verb “وَنُقَلِّبُكَ”.
rows.anchor: أنه قرىء { * ونقلبك }

rows.speaker: الرافضة
rows.claim: The Rāfiḍa argue that the Prophet’s ancestors were believers and take the verse to allow God to have transferred his soul from one prostrating ancestor to another.
rows.anchor: الرافضة ذهبوا إلى أن آباء النبي صلى الله عليه وسلم كانوا مؤمنين وتمسكوا في ذلك بهذه الآية

rows.speaker: النبي صلى الله عليه وسلم
rows.claim: The Rāfiḍa also cite the report that the Prophet was continually transferred from pure loins to pure wombs, reasoning that every unbeliever is impure; the verse is in 9:28. Rāzī gives no grading.
rows.anchor: قوله عليه السلام : ( لم أزل أنقل من أصلاب الطاهرين إلى أرحام الطاهرات )

rows.speaker: الرافضة
rows.claim: To answer the reference to Abraham’s father Āzar, they say “father” can mean uncle: Jacob’s sons call Ishmael their father though he was their uncle, and the Prophet called al-ʿAbbās “my father.”
rows.anchor: الرافضة ذهبوا إلى أن آباء النبي صلى الله عليه وسلم كانوا مؤمنين وتمسكوا في ذلك بهذه الآية

rows.speaker: الرافضة
rows.claim: They also allow “father” to mean a maternal grandfather, citing Jesus’ inclusion among Abraham’s descendants although Abraham was his maternal grandfather.
rows.anchor: الرافضة ذهبوا إلى أن آباء النبي صلى الله عليه وسلم كانوا مؤمنين وتمسكوا في ذلك بهذه الآية

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Rāzī holds to the apparent sense of “his father Āzar”; the Rāfiḍa’s explanation shifts the word away from its apparent meaning.
rows.anchor: بقوله تعالى : { لابيه ءازر } وما ذكروه صرف للفظ عن ظاهره

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Rāzī rejects taking the shared expression in all its possible senses at once, since an ambiguous word cannot carry all of them together.
rows.anchor: لما بينا أن حمل المشترك على كل معانيه غير جائز

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The report about pure loins and wombs is a solitary report and therefore cannot outweigh the Qur’an.
rows.anchor: وأما الحديث فهو خبر واحد فلا يعارض القرآن

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: ʿAmāh means confusion and hesitation, like the state of someone lost from the road.
rows.anchor: فالعمه التحير والتردد كما يكون حال الضال عن الطريق

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: One view takes the severe punishment as killing and captivity at Badr.
rows.anchor: الأول : أنه القتل والأسر يوم بدر

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Another view takes it as any worldly or afterlife punishment, with “evil” meaning its severity and greatness.
rows.anchor: مطلق العذاب سواء كان في الدنيا أو في الآخرة والمراد بالسوء شدته وعظمه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: One view says they are the greatest losers because they lose themselves: deprived of health and safety in this life, they face great punishment in the next.
rows.anchor: لا خسران أعظم من أن يخسر المرء نفسه بأن يسلب عنه الصحة والسلامة في الدنيا ويسلم في الآخرة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Another view says each accountable person had a place assigned in Paradise if obedient; by disobeying, they lost that place and were assigned elsewhere.
rows.anchor: المراد أنهم خسروا منازلهم في الجنة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Moses had lost the road; the passage omits that he saw the fire and turned toward it, then spoke to his family to guide their way.
rows.anchor: فالخبر ما يخبر به عن حال الطريق لأنه كان قد ضل

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Shihāb is a flame, and qabas is fire taken from another fire; shihāb is annexed to qabas because it may be a firebrand or something else.
rows.anchor: فالشهاب الشعلة والقبس النار المقبوسة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: With tanwīn, qabas is analyzed as an apposition or adjective, since the preceding word already conveys the sense of taking fire.
rows.anchor: ومن قرأ بالتنوين جعل القبس بدلا أو صفة لما فيه من معنى القبس

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The hopeful wording does not conflict with the report that Moses had completed his term: a person with strong hope may say something will happen while still allowing failure.
rows.anchor: قد يقول الراجي إذا قوي رجاؤه سأفعل كذا وسيكون كذا مع تجويزه الخيبة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The future particle is a promise to his family that he will bring something back, even if he is delayed or the way is distant.
rows.anchor: جوابه : عدة منه لأهله أنه يأتيهم به وإن أبطأ أو كانت المسافة بعيدة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: “Or” expresses his hope to obtain at least one of the two things—directions or fire—relying on God’s custom not to deprive a servant of both.
rows.anchor: بنى الرجاء على أنه إن لم يظفر بهذين المقصودين ظفر بأحدهما

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The phrase means “so that you may warm yourselves,” implying that they needed a fire because it was cold.
rows.anchor: فالمعنى لكي تصطلون وذلك يدل على حاجة بهم إلى الاصطلاء

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: An is explanatory because a call contains the sense of speech; the meaning is that he was told, “Blessed is …”.
rows.anchor: هي المفسرة لأن النداء فيه معنى القول

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: One reported interpretation takes “the one in the fire” as God, with fire meaning light and those around it meaning angels; Rāzī calls the Ibn ʿAbbās report fabricated.
rows.anchor: وهو مروي عن ابن عباس رضي الله عنهما وإن كنا نقطع بأن هذه الرواية موضوعة مختلفة

rows.speaker: قتادة والزجاج
rows.claim: Qatāda and al-Zajjāj take the one in the fire to be God’s light and those around it to be the angels.
rows.anchor: هو نور الله ، { ومن حولها } الملائكة ، وهو مروي عن قتادة والزجاج

rows.speaker: الجبائي
rows.claim: Al-Jubbāʾī says God spoke to Moses through speech heard from the tree in the blessed spot; God created the speech in the tree, which was in the fire, while angels were around it.
rows.anchor: أن الله تعالى ناداه بكلام سمعه من الشجرة في البقعة المباركة فكانت الشجرة محلا للكلام

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Rāzī finds the nearer view that Moses is the one in the fire because he was close to it, while those around it are angels; proximity can be described as being inside something.
rows.anchor: وهذا أقرب لأن القريب من الشيء قد يقال إنه فيه

rows.speaker: صاحب الكشاف
rows.claim: Al-Zamakhsharī takes the phrase as referring to the place of the fire and the area around that place, the blessed spot mentioned in 28:30.
rows.anchor: أي من في مكان النار ومن حول مكانها هي البقعة التي حصلت فيها

rows.speaker: أبي
rows.claim: Ubayy’s readings include “Blessed is the earth and what is around it” and “Blessed is the fire.”
rows.anchor: ويدل عليه قراءة أبي ( تباركت الأرض ومن حولها ) وعنه أيضا ( بوركت النار )

words: بُورِكَ مَن فِى ٱلنَّارِ وَمَنْ حَوْلَهَا
rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The spot and those around it were blessed because God spoke to Moses there, appointed him a messenger, and showed him miracles; Syria is blessed in 21:71 for this reason.
rows.anchor: حدوث هذا الأمر العظيم فيها وهو تكليم الله موسى عليه السلام وجعله رسولا

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Syria deserves blessing as the birthplace of prophets, the place where revelation descends, and their resting place in life and death.
rows.anchor: مبعث الأنبياء صلوات الله عليهم ، ومهبط الوحي وكفاتهم

words: بُورِكَ مَن فِى ٱلنَّارِ وَمَنْ حَوْلَهَا
rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The blessing announcement prepares for Moses’ private conversation by signaling that an immense event has occurred, whose blessing spreads through all Syria.
rows.anchor: يدل على أنه قد قضى أمر عظيم تنتشر البركة منه في أرض الشام كلها

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The glorification has two purposes: to deny what does not befit God’s essence or wisdom, preparing for the proof of Moses’ mission, and to announce that the Lord of the worlds wills and creates this great event.
rows.anchor: نزه نفسه عما لا يليق به في ذاته وحكمته ليكون ذلك مقدمة في صحة رسالة موسى عليه السلام

rows.speaker: صاحب الكشاف
rows.claim: Al-Zamakhsharī allows the pronoun in inna to be a pronoun of the matter, with “I am God” as subject and predicate, or to refer back to what preceded it.
rows.anchor: يجوز أن يكون ضمير الشأن و

rows.speaker: صاحب الكشاف
rows.claim: On the second parsing, “God” explains “I,” and “Mighty, Wise” are identifying attributes.
rows.anchor: يعني أن مكلمك أنا والله بيان لأنا

rows.speaker: صاحب الكشاف
rows.claim: The names prepare for a miracle: God is powerful to do what seems impossible, such as turning a staff into a snake, and acts with wisdom and governance.
rows.anchor: وهذا تمهيد لما أراد أن يظهره على يده من المعجزة يريد أنا القوي القادر على ما يبعد من الأوهام

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Sunnis offer two ways Moses could know the caller was God: he heard speech unlike letters or sounds and knew necessarily it was God’s attribute, or he heard a voice from the tree.
rows.anchor: أنه سمع الكلام المنزه عن مشابهة الحروف والأصوات فعلم بالضرورة

rows.speaker: أئمة ما وراء النهر
rows.claim: Transoxanian imams say Moses heard a voice from the tree, then ask what established that the caller was God.
rows.anchor: قول أئمة ما وراء النهر وهو أنه عليه السلام سمع الصوت من الشجرة

rows.speaker: أئمة ما وراء النهر
rows.claim: Their first proof—that a human cannot make a call from fire or a tree—is weak, since Satan could enter the fire or tree and call.
rows.anchor: لأن أحدا منا لا يقدر عليه وهو ضعف لاحتمال أن يقال الشيطان دخل في النار والشجرة

rows.speaker: أئمة ما وراء النهر
rows.claim: Their second proof, that the voice’s magnitude must be miraculous, is weak because the powers of angels and devils are unknown and could account for any magnitude.
rows.anchor: وهو أيضا ضعيف لأنا لا نعرف مقادير قوى الملائكة والشياطين فلا قدر إلا ويجوز صدوره منهم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The soundest proof is an accompanying miracle: the fire burned in a green tree without consuming it.
rows.anchor: إن النار كانت مشتعلة في شجرة خضراء لم تحترق

none: The segment contains only a quotation of verses 27:10-14, with no commentary.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: “Throw down your staff” is coordinated with the blessing announcement in 27:8; both clauses explain the call to Moses.
rows.anchor: وأن ألق عصاك ، كلاهما تفسير لنودي

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Jānn is a small snake, named so because it hides itself from people.
rows.anchor: سميت جانا ، لأنها تستتر عن الناس

rows.speaker: الحسن
rows.claim: Al-Ḥasan reads jānn without tanwīn, following a dialect that avoids the meeting of two sukūns, as in “shaʾba” and “daʾba.”
rows.anchor: وقرأ الحسن { جان } على لغة من يهرب من التقاء الساكنين

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Lam yuʿaqqib means he did not return; the idiom describes a fighter turning back after fleeing.
rows.anchor: معناه لم يرجع ، يقال عقب المقاتل

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Moses fled because he thought the snake’s appearance meant something was intended against him.
rows.anchor: وإنما خاف لظنه أن ذلك لأمر أريد به

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: One interpretation limits the messengers’ lack of fear to the occasions when God commands them to display a miracle; otherwise a messenger can certainly feel fear.
rows.anchor: وقال بعضهم : المراد إني إذا أمرتهم بإظهار معجز في

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The exception means “but whoever has done wrong”; it can refer to prophets’ leaving the better course or committing a minor sin.
rows.anchor: معناه لكن من ظلم وهو محمول على ما يصدر من الأنبياء من ترك الأفضل أو الصغيرة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Another possibility is a subtle allusion to what happened to Moses.
rows.anchor: ويحتمل أن يكون المقصود منه التعريض بما وجد من موسى

rows.speaker: الحسن
rows.claim: Al-Ḥasan says Moses was among those who did wrong by killing the Copt, then repented, citing his prayer that God forgive him for wronging himself; Rāzī gives no grading.
rows.anchor: قال الحسن رحمه الله : كان والله موسى ممن ظلم بقتل القبطي

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A reading has “ألا من ظلم,” with the attention particle alā.
rows.anchor: وقرىء ( ألا من ظلم ) بحرف التنبيه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The good is repentance and the evil is the sin.
rows.anchor: فالمراد حسن التوبة وسوء الذنب

rows.speaker: أبو بكر عن عاصم
rows.claim: Abū Bakr’s transmission from ʿĀṣim reads ḥasanan with the indicated vocalization.
rows.anchor: وعن أبي بكر في رواية عاصم ( حسنا )

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: “Put your hand into your breast opening” begins an independent clause; its preposition attaches to an omitted phrase, with the sense “go with nine signs to Pharaoh.”
rows.anchor: حرف الجر فيه يتعلق بمحذوف

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: One objection says Moses’ signs totaled eleven: hand and staff, plus nine—flood, locusts, lice, frogs, blood, obliteration, famine in the countryside, and crop loss.
rows.anchor: اثنتان منها اليد والعصا

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The signs are described as seeing, though sight belongs to those who contemplate them; alternatively, their clarity makes them seem to see and find guidance.
rows.anchor: وهو في الحقيقة لمتأملها

rows.speaker: علي بن الحسين وقتادة
rows.claim: ʿAlī ibn al-Ḥusayn and Qatāda read mubsira as a form denoting a place where much seeing occurs, like majbana and makhbala.
rows.anchor: وقرأ علي بن الحسين وقتادة { مبصرة } وهو نحو مجبنة

words: إِنَّ ٱلْمُلُوكَ إِذَا دَخَلُوا۟ قَرْيَةً أَفْسَدُوهَا
rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: After her council’s response, the queen gives her judgment: kings who conquer a town by force destroy it and humiliate its honored people, describing war’s consequence.
rows.anchor: وهو أن الملوك إذا دخلوا قرية بالقهر

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Although it could be God’s approving comment, Rāzī finds it more likely to be the queen’s own words, reinforcing her description of kings.
rows.anchor: اختلفوا أهو من كلامها أو من كلام الله تعالى كالتصويب لها والأقرب أنه من كلامها

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The Qur’an gives no details about the gift, although people have speculated extensively about what it contained.
rows.anchor: أما الكلام في صفة الهدية فالناس أكثروا فيها لكن لا ذكر لها في الكتاب

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Her waiting to see what the messengers bring back shows she does not trust that the gift will be accepted and allows for refusal; she wants to discover Solomon’s aim.
rows.anchor: أنها لم تثق بالقبول وجوزت الرد

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Solomon’s question shows how little he cared about the offered wealth.
rows.anchor: فأظهر بهذا الكلام قلة الاكتراث بذلك المال

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: One reading takes hadiyya as the gift itself, a noun that may be attributed to giver or recipient; here it is attributed to its recipients.
rows.anchor: الهدية اسم للمهدي ، كما أن العطية اسم للمعطي

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: On that reading, God gave Solomon the supreme happiness of religion and abundant worldly goods, so a gift could not tempt him; the queen’s people rejoice in gifts, unlike him.
rows.anchor: آتاني الدين الذي هو السعادة القصوى

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A second view says they rejoice because they were able to give a gift like this one.
rows.anchor: بل أنتم بهديتكم هذه التي أهديتموها تفرحون من حيث إنكم قدرتم على إهداء مثلها

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A third view takes Solomon to mean that they should take their gift back and rejoice in it.
rows.anchor: بل أنتم من حقكم أن تأخذوا هديتكم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The command to return may address the messenger, or the hoopoe carrying another letter.
rows.anchor: ارجع خطاب للرسول ، وقيل للهدهد

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Qubl means capacity or resistance: they cannot face or withstand the forces.
rows.anchor: حقيقة القبل المقاومة والمقابلة

rows.speaker: ابن مسعود
rows.claim: Ibn Masʿūd reads “they have no capacity against them.”
rows.anchor: وقرأ ابن مسعود : ( لا قبل لهم بهم )

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The pronoun in “from it” refers to Sheba.
rows.anchor: والضمير في ( منها ) لسبأ

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Dhull means losing their former honor and kingship; ṣaghār means capture and enslavement, not merely becoming commoners after being kings.
rows.anchor: أن يذهب عنهم ما كان عندهم من العز والملك

none: The segment contains only a quotation of verses 27:38-40, with no commentary.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Iltiqāṭ means finding or picking something up without having sought it; the family of Pharaoh here means his female servants.
rows.anchor: فالالتقاط إصابة الشيء من غير طلب

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The commonly held view takes the lām as one of consequence; a purpose reading would conflict with Pharaoh’s wife calling Moses a comfort and God’s saying He cast love on him, as in 7:179.
rows.anchor: المشهور أن هذه اللام يراد بها العاقبة

rows.speaker: صاحب الكشاف
rows.claim: Rāzī prefers al-Zamakhsharī’s account: this is figurative purpose, since an object’s eventual outcome is treated as its aim, like calling a brave person a lion.
rows.anchor: هذه اللام هي لام التعليل على سبيل المجاز

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The poem “They bear children for death and build for ruin” illustrates a purpose construction whose result is the opposite of the apparent intent.
rows.anchor: وقوله الشاعر : لدوا للموت وابنوا للخراب

rows.speaker: حمزة والكسائي
rows.claim: Ḥamza and al-Kisāʾī read ḥuznan with ḍamma on ḥāʾ and sukūn on zāy; the others read ḥazanan with fatḥa on both, two dialect forms like saqm and saqam.
rows.anchor: قرأ حمزة والكسائي ( حزنا ) بضم الحاء وسكون الزاي

rows.speaker: الحسن
rows.claim: Al-Ḥasan says khāṭiʾīn here does not mean sinning: they did not realize this child would take their kingdom.
rows.anchor: قال الحسن معنى { كانوا خاطئين } ليس من الخطيئة

rows.speaker: جمهور المفسرين
rows.claim: Most exegetes understand that Pharaoh’s people were wrong in disbelief and oppression, so God made them raise their enemy, the cause of their destruction, themselves.
rows.anchor: وأما جمهور المفسرين فقالوا معناه كانوا خاطئين فيما كانوا عليه من الكفر والظلم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A shortened reading, khāṭīn, lightens khāṭiʾīn and means those who miss the right and go toward error.
rows.anchor: تخفيف خاطئين أي خاطين الصواب إلى الخطأ

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: God made Moses a comfort and delight to both Pharaoh’s wife and Pharaoh.
rows.anchor: وبين تعالى أنها التقطته ليكون قرة عين لها وله جميعا

rows.speaker: ابن إسحق
rows.claim: Ibn Isḥāq says God placed love for Moses in her heart because of his beauty, the light she saw on opening the chest, his sucking his finger, and the healing of Pharaoh’s daughter’s leprosy by his saliva; it is also said she had no child. No grading is given.
rows.anchor: قال ابن إسحق إن الله تعالى ألقى محبته في قلبها لأنه كان في وجهه ملاحة

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: Ibn ʿAbbās says Pharaoh replied that the child could be his wife’s comfort but he had no need of him; the Prophet swore that if Pharaoh had acknowledged him as his own comfort, God would have guided him as He guided her. No grading is given.
rows.anchor: قال ابن عباس لما قالت : { فرعون قرة عين لي ولك } فقال فرعون يكون لك

rows.speaker: صاحب الكشاف
rows.claim: Al-Zamakhsharī parses “a comfort to the eye” as the predicate of an omitted subject; making it the subject with “do not kill him” as predicate is weak, and Ibn Masʿūd’s reading supports the predicate analysis.
rows.anchor: قرة عين } خبر مبتدأ محذوف ولا يقوى أن يجعل مبتدأ

rows.speaker: ابن مسعود
rows.claim: Ibn Masʿūd reads “Do not kill him; a comfort to my eye and yours,” placing the prohibition first as evidence for the predicate parsing.
rows.anchor: وقراءة ابن مسعود دليل على أنه خبر ، قرأ { لا تقتلوه قرة عين لي ولك }

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The queen hopes Moses may benefit them or that they may adopt him, since he is worthy to be taken as a son.
rows.anchor: المرأة { عسى أن ينفعنا } فنصيب

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The day after the Egyptian died from Moses’ blow, Moses feared that his identity as killer would be exposed and that he would be sought, so he left in secret.
rows.anchor: أصبح موسى عليه السلام من غد ذلك اليوم خائفا من أن يظهر أنه هو القاتل

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The one who had sought his help was the Israelite; to “cry for help” means asking for aid with shouting and screaming.
rows.anchor: وهو الإسرائيلي { بالامس يستصرخه } يطلب نصرته بصياح وصراخ

rows.speaker: أهل اللغة
rows.claim: Linguists allow ghawī to mean “one who misleads,” so Moses means the man caused trouble with his people the day before, or to mean “astray.”
rows.anchor: قال أهل اللغة الغوي يجوز أن يكون فعيلا بمعنى مفعل

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Those who challenge prophetic impeccability object that Moses should not call a fellow Israelite who sought his help manifestly misguided.
rows.anchor: من قدح في عصمة الأنبياء عليهم السلام

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: First answer: Moses’ people were rough and uncouth, as shown by their later demand for an idol after witnessing signs; “manifestly misguided” describes that disposition.
rows.anchor: أن قوم موسى عليه السلام كانوا غلاظا جفاة ألا ترى إلى قولهم بعد مشاهدة الآيات

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Second answer: someone who repeatedly quarrels so that his opponent cannot be stopped from harming him has departed from the path of sound judgment.
rows.anchor: إنما سماه غويا لأن من تكثر منه المخاصمة على وجه يتعذر عليه دفع خصمه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: One view makes the Israelite the speaker: after Moses called him misguided and angrily moved to strike, he thought Moses meant to kill him; only he knew of the previous killing, so he exposed it and increased Moses’ fear.
rows.anchor: فقال بعضهم لما خاطب موسى الإسرائيلي بأنه غوي ورآه على غضب ظن لما هم بالبطش

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The other view makes the Copt the speaker, already informed by the Israelite; Rāzī prefers it because the next clause’s “tyrant on earth” accusation suits an unbeliever, and the verse attributes the speech to the enemy of both.
rows.anchor: قول القبطي ، وقد كان عرف القصة من الإسرائيلي

words: إِن تُرِيدُ إِلَّآ أَن تَكُونَ جَبَّارًۭا فِى ٱلْأَرْضِ
rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: One definition of jabbār is someone who unjustly does whatever he wants by beating and killing, without considering consequences or choosing the better response.
rows.anchor: الجبار الذي يفعل ما يريد من الضرب والقتل بظلم لا ينظر في العواقب

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Another definition is an arrogant person who will not submit to anyone’s command.
rows.anchor: وقيل المتعظم الذي لا يتواضع لأمر أحد

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: After this incident, the news spread through the city, reached Pharaoh, and they resolved to kill Moses.
rows.anchor: ولما وقعت هذه الواقعة انتشر الحديث في المدينة وانتهى إلى فرعون وهموا بقتله

rows.speaker: صاحب الكشاف
rows.claim: Al-Zamakhsharī says yasʿā may be a modifier of “a man” or a circumstantial accusative, since “from the farthest part of the city” has already specified him.
rows.anchor: قال صاحب ( الكشاف ) يسعى يجوز ارتفاعه وصفا لرجل

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Iʾtimār means consultation: two people each advise the other or point him toward an action; here the chiefs are consulting about Moses.
rows.anchor: والائتمار التشاور يقال الرجلان ( يتآمران ) يأتمران

rows.speaker: جمهور المفسرين
rows.claim: Most exegetes identify the man as the believer from Pharaoh’s family, who hurries out of concern to warn Moses that the chiefs are consulting to kill him.
rows.anchor: وأكثر المفسرين على أن هذا الرجل مؤمن آل فرعون

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Moses left fearing for his life from Pharaoh’s people, watching to see whether they would pursue and seize him.
rows.anchor: أي خائفا على نفسه من آل فرعون ينتظر هل يلحقه طلب فيؤخذ

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Knowing there was no refuge except God, Moses sought refuge with Him and asked to be saved from the oppressors.
rows.anchor: ثم التجأ إلى الله تعالى لعلمه بأنه لا ملجأ سواه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Rāzī says this shows Moses’ killing of the Copt was not a sin: otherwise Moses would be the oppressor, not the people seeking to kill him in retribution.
rows.anchor: وهذا يدل على أن قتله لذلك القبطي لم يكن ذنبا
